name: Glibenclamide
route_note: oral tablet once or twice daily with breakfast; micronised formulation in some markets

discovery.note: Developed jointly as a potent second-generation sulfonylurea.

tagline: A potent second-generation sulfonylurea that closes beta-cell potassium channels
summary: Glibenclamide (glyburide in the US) is a sulfonylurea that stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells. It is inexpensive and effective but carries a higher risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia than newer sulfonylureas, particularly in older people and those with kidney impairment.
mechanism: Glibenclamide binds the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1 (ABCC8), the regulatory subunit of the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel in beta-cell membranes. Channel closure depolarises the cell, opens voltage-gated calcium channels and triggers exocytosis of insulin granules, independent of the prevailing glucose level.

Because the effect does not switch off when glucose is low, hypoglycaemia is the main hazard. The same mechanism lets high-dose oral glibenclamide replace insulin in many people with neonatal diabetes caused by activating KCNJ11 or ABCC8 mutations.
uses: Neonatal diabetes due to KATP channel mutations (off-label)

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Glibenclamide is developed by Boehringer Mannheim with Hoechst.

history.title: Launch
history.detail: Marketed in Europe as Euglucon and Daonil.

history.title: US approval
history.detail: FDA approves glyburide as Diabeta and Micronase.

history.title: Neonatal diabetes
history.detail: Studies (NEJM 2006) show sulfonylureas can replace insulin in neonatal diabetes due to Kir6.2 mutations.

history.title: Gestational diabetes debate
history.detail: Trials and meta-analyses comparing glibenclamide with insulin and metformin in pregnancy lead several guidelines to prefer insulin or metformin.

pk.metabolism: hepatic CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 to weakly active metabolites

safety.boxed_warning: US labels for sulfonylureas carry a special warning on increased cardiovascular mortality based on the 1970 UGDP study of tolbutamide.

facts: Glibenclamide is known as glyburide in the United States and Canada.
Oral sulfonylureas allow many children with KCNJ11 neonatal diabetes to stop insulin injections.

references.title: Pearson ER et al. Switching from insulin to oral sulfonylureas in neonatal diabetes (NEJM 2006)
